title: Statements and Conclusions — Critical Filtering
tagline: Year 3 — Accept only what the statement itself supports: avoid outside knowledge, over-reading and reversed conditions

introduction.overview: In a statements-and-conclusions question you are given a short statement and some conclusions, and you must decide which conclusions follow. The central skill is critical filtering: a conclusion follows only if it is directly supported by the statement, with no help from outside knowledge. This chapter teaches how to filter out four kinds of bad conclusion: unsupported additions, reversed conditions, over-generalisations and extra assumptions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Statement-and-conclusion items appear in most logical-reasoning sections of company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading a report or a contract and deciding what it actually commits to uses the same filter.

learningObjectives: Separate what is stated from what is assumed

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A conclusion follows if the statement guarantees it. If the statement leaves it open, it does not follow.

coreDefinitions: Directly supported: the conclusion is said or logically forced by the statement.
Reversed condition: turning "if A then B" into "if B then A".
Over-generalisation: moving from some or most to all.
Outside knowledge: a fact that is true in the world but not stated.
Contrapositive: "if A then B" is equivalent to "if not B then not A".
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Treat the statement as the only fact in the universe. If you need anything else to reach a conclusion, it does not follow.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Ask for each conclusion: "Does the statement alone make this true?" Reject on any of four grounds: added fact, reversed condition, over-generalisation, or extra assumption.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Direct support
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Employees got a bonus ⇒ Ravi got one

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Reversed condition
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If A then B ⇏ if B then A

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Contrapositive
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If A then B ⇒ if not B then not A

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Either-or
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A or B, not A ⇒ B

mainNarrative: The statement "All the employees of the firm were given a bonus" supports "Ravi, an employee, got a bonus" directly. It contradicts "Some employees did not get a bonus". So only the first conclusion follows.

Reversed conditions are the commonest trap. "The company will hire only graduates" tells you what is necessary for hiring, not that every graduate is hired. "A non-graduate will not be hired" follows; "All graduates will be hired" does not.
Numbers allow computation but not outside facts. If 36 of 40 students passed, then 4 did not pass is a valid conclusion. But "the 4 who failed were absent" is not.
Either-or statements allow elimination. "Either the printer is faulty or the cable is loose" with "the cable is tight" gives "the printer is faulty".
A conclusion that reaches beyond the subject of the statement, such as other cities, other years or other products, usually fails because the statement does not mention them.

deepDiveAspects.title: Necessary vs sufficient
deepDiveAspects.content: "Only" and "must" mark necessary conditions; they do not promise the outcome.

deepDiveAspects.title: Either I or II
deepDiveAspects.content: When the two conclusions are complementary (one the opposite of the other) and the statement is silent, "either I or II follows" would apply; this chapter uses only the four standard options.

solvedExamples.title: Reversed condition
solvedExamples.question: Statement: The company will hire only graduates for the post. Conclusion: All graduates will be hired. Does it follow?

steps.title: Test
steps.explanation: It does not promise that every graduate is hired.

solvedExamples.title: Numbers
solvedExamples.question: Statement: 36 of the 40 students in the class passed. Conclusion: Some students did not pass. Does it follow?

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.explanation: So some students did not pass.

solvedExamples.title: Either-or
solvedExamples.question: Statement: Either the printer is faulty or the cable is loose; the cable is tight. Conclusion: The printer is faulty. Does it follow?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: One option of the either-or is removed.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: For each conclusion ask whether the statement alone makes it true; reject added facts, reversed conditions and over-generalisations.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: If a conclusion needs an extra fact, drop it.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Underline quantity words: all, some, only, most.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Two-conclusion items reward checking each one separately.

easy.question:
Statement: All the employees of the firm were given a bonus this year.

Conclusions:
I. Ravi, an employee of the firm, received a bonus this year.
II. Some employees of the firm did not receive a bonus this year.

Which of the following is correct?
easy.explanation: The statement says every employee got a bonus, so Ravi did too (I follows) and no employee missed out (II contradicts it). Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

easy.question:
Statement: The shop remains closed on Sundays.

Conclusions:
I. The shop is open on Mondays.
II. The shop does no business on Sundays.

Which of the following is correct?
easy.explanation: A shop that is closed on Sundays does no business on Sundays (II follows). The statement says nothing about Mondays, so I does not follow. Answer: Only conclusion II follows.

easy.question:
Statement: In a class of 40 students, 36 passed the test.

Conclusions:
I. Some students did not pass the test.
II. Every student passed the test.

Which of the following is correct?
easy.explanation: 40 − 36 = 4 students did not pass, so I follows and II is false. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

intermediate.question:
Statement: Some cars in the showroom are electric, and all electric cars have zero tailpipe emissions.

Conclusions:
I. Some cars in the showroom have zero tailpipe emissions.
II. All cars in the showroom are electric.

Which of the following is correct?
intermediate.explanation: The electric cars in the showroom have zero tailpipe emissions, so I follows. Only "some" cars are electric, so II does not follow. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

intermediate.question:
Statement: Only members of the club may use its swimming pool.

Conclusions:
I. A person who is not a member cannot use the pool.
II. Every member uses the pool.

Which of the following is correct?
intermediate.explanation: "Only members" makes membership necessary, so I follows. Nothing says members actually use it, so II does not follow. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

intermediate.question:
Statement: The price of petrol was increased by 10% last month.

Conclusions:
I. The price of petrol before last month was lower than it is now.
II. The price of diesel also rose last month.

Which of the following is correct?
intermediate.explanation: A 10% increase makes the new price higher than the old, so I follows. Diesel is not mentioned, so II does not follow. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

advanced.question:
Statement: The government has announced a subsidy for farmers who own less than 2 hectares of land.

Conclusions:
I. A farmer with 1.5 hectares of land is eligible for the subsidy.
II. A farmer with 3 hectares of land will not receive the subsidy.

Which of the following is correct?
advanced.explanation: 1.5 is less than 2, so I follows. The statement does not say that others are excluded, so II does not follow. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

advanced.question:
Statement: Of the 120 candidates who appeared, 90 passed the written test, 60 passed the interview, and 40 passed both.

Conclusions:
I. Exactly 10 candidates passed neither.
II. Exactly 50 candidates passed only the written test.

Which of the following is correct?
advanced.explanation: Passed at least one = 90 + 60 − 40 = 110, so 120 − 110 = 10 passed neither (I). Only the written test: 90 − 40 = 50 (II). Both follow. Answer: Both conclusions follow.

placementStyle.question:
Statement: If the signal is red, the car stops. The car did not stop.

Conclusions:
I. The signal was not red.
II. The signal was red.

Which of the following is correct?
placementStyle.explanation: The contrapositive of "if red then stops" is "if not stopped then not red", so I follows and II contradicts it. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

placementStyle.question:
Statement: Every applicant who clears the test is called for an interview. Some applicants who were called for an interview were rejected.

Conclusions:
I. Some applicants who cleared the test were rejected.
II. Some applicants who were called for an interview did not clear the test.

Which of the following is correct?
placementStyle.explanation: The statement does not say that only those who cleared the test are called, so the rejected interviewees may not have cleared it. Neither conclusion is forced. Answer: Neither conclusion follows.

placementStyle.question:
Statement: Either the printer is faulty or the cable is loose. The cable has been checked and is tight.

Conclusions:
I. The printer is faulty.
II. The printer is not faulty.

Which of the following is correct?
placementStyle.explanation: The cable is not loose, so the printer must be faulty. I follows and II contradicts it. Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

quickFormulas: If A then B ⇒ if not B then not A

selfCheckQuestions: Can I spot a reversed condition?
